Amaziah
am-a-ZYE-uh
proper noun (figure)
Hebrew Amatsyahu (H558) — "Yahweh is mighty" or "Yahweh has strength." From amats ("to be strong, to prevail") + Yah (the divine name).

Biblical Definition

Amaziah (c. 796 — 767 BC) was the ninth king of Judah (2 Kings 14:1-22; 2 Chronicles 25), son of Joash whose own assassination he avenged but whose covenant integrity he could not sustain. Ascended the throne at twenty-five and reigned twenty-nine years — a long reign by Judean standards — but the canonical assessment is mixed: "He did that which was right in the sight of the LORD, yet not with a perfect heart" (2 Chr 25:2). Three episodes define his record. First, the execution of his father's assassins, carried out with deliberate restraint that obeyed Deuteronomy 24:16 ("The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, neither shall the children be put to death for the fathers") and refused the customary ancient-Near-Eastern practice of executing the assassin's children with him (2 Kings 14:5-6) — a striking moment of Mosaic-law fidelity in a small executive matter. Second, his Edomite campaign: hired one hundred thousand Israelite mercenaries from the northern kingdom for a hundred talents of silver, then dismissed them on prophetic counsel and won the Valley of Salt against ten thousand Edomites with Judahite forces alone (2 Chr 25:5-13); but immediately after the victory he brought the captured Edomite gods to Jerusalem and worshiped them — an inexplicable apostasy that the chapter explicitly highlights ("He brought the gods of the children of Seir, and set them up to be his gods, and bowed down himself before them, and burned incense unto them" — 2 Chr 25:14). Third, his ill-fated challenge to King Joash of Israel: pride after the Edomite victory led him to pick a fight he could not win; he was captured, Jerusalem was sacked, and the temple's gold and vessels were carried to Samaria. He was eventually assassinated at Lachish, a fugitive from his own people. His name — "Yahweh is mighty" — was vindicated in his early Edomite victory and indicted by his later worship of the very gods he had defeated.

Webster 1828 Definition

Ninth king of Judah (c. 796-767 BC); son of Joash; reigned 29 years; executed his father's assassins under Mosaic-law restraint (Deut 24:16); won the Valley of Salt against Edom (2 Chr 25); then worshiped captured Edomite gods and was defeated and humiliated by King Joash of Israel.

AMAZIAH, proper noun. Hebrew Amatsyahu (H558) — "Yahweh is mighty," from amats ("to be strong") + Yah.

Ninth king of Judah (c. 796-767 BC); son of Joash; reigned 29 years.

Three signature episodes: principled execution of his father's assassins (2 Kings 14:5-6 / 2 Chr 25:3-4); Valley-of-Salt victory over Edom (2 Chr 25:5-13); apostasy of worshiping captured Edomite gods (2 Chr 25:14) and disastrous war with King Joash of Israel (2 Chr 25:17-24).

Assassinated at Lachish (2 Chr 25:27).

Key Scripture

2 Chronicles 25:2 — "And he did that which was right in the sight of the LORD, but not with a perfect heart."

2 Chronicles 25:14-15 — "Now it came to pass, after that Amaziah was come from the slaughter of the Edomites, that he brought the gods of the children of Seir, and set them up to be his gods, and bowed down himself before them, and burned incense unto them. Wherefore the anger of the LORD was kindled against Amaziah..."

Deuteronomy 24:16 — "The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, neither shall the children be put to death for the fathers: every man shall be put to death for his own sin."

Proverbs 16:18 — "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall."

Modern Corruption

Amaziah is corrupted when his early Deuteronomic restraint with his father's assassins is read as the totality of his record without the later apostasy that defined his reign, when the absurd Edomite-gods episode is treated as merely strange without the doctrinal weight Scripture gives it, or when the Israelite-mercenary dismissal is read tactically rather than as obedience to a prophet's word.

expand to see more

Selective-virtue reading. Some readings of Amaziah lift the Deuteronomy-24:16 restraint with his father's assassins as evidence of his deep Mosaic-law obedience. The chapter as a whole resists this selective lift: the same king who refused to kill children for their fathers' crimes brought enemy gods home and worshiped them, then went to war out of pride and lost his kingdom's wealth. The verse-by-verse Mosaic-law detail in one matter is not equivalent to wholehearted obedience in the rest of life. The Chronicler's summary verdict ("right in the sight of the LORD, yet not with a perfect heart") refuses the selective virtue.

Edomite-gods absurdity. The episode in 2 Chr 25:14 — bringing the gods of a people he had just defeated and worshiping them — is so theologically absurd that some modern readers treat it as embellishment. The Chronicler's prophet (anonymous) recognized the absurdity in real time and asked the king bluntly: "Why hast thou sought after the gods of the people, which could not deliver their own people out of thine hand?" (2 Chr 25:15). The Chronicler is making a doctrinal point about idolatry: it is not rational; it is the heart's foolishness, defended even against the obvious failure of the false god to save its own people.

Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Amatsyahu (H558) — "Yahweh is mighty," from amats + Yah. The ninth king of Judah; son of Joash; reigned 29 years.

Hebrew Amatsyahu (H558) — "Yahweh is mighty" or "Yahweh has strength"

Compound: amats ("to be strong, to prevail") + Yah (the divine name)

Ninth king of the divided southern kingdom of Judah (c. 796-767 BC)

Son of Joash; father of Uzziah/Azariah (his successor)

Two main accounts: 2 Kings 14:1-22 (briefer) and 2 Chronicles 25 (fuller)

Usage

"Amaziah — "Yahweh is mighty"; the ninth king of Judah who started with Deuteronomic restraint and ended worshiping captured Edomite gods."

"Right in the sight of the LORD, yet not with a perfect heart — the Chronicler's summary verdict."

"His career is a sustained meditation on the difference between partial obedience and wholehearted covenant fidelity."
